Live Analysis walkthrough
xrefcode.com / docs / cli / live-heap

$ xref live heap

by Alexander Panasenko · xrefcode.com
On this page
  1. Usage
  2. Arguments and options
  3. Examples
  4. Reading the output
  5. How bytes are attributed
  6. Limits

Find which call stacks hold the anonymous memory of a running process. xref follows the memory syscalls of every thread (mmap, munmap, mremap, brk, mprotect) through kernel tracepoints, copies the user stack at each one that maps memory, unwinds it from .eh_frame like live profile, and reports the stacks by the bytes they still hold. There is no uprobe on malloc, so the process keeps its speed even with millions of allocations per second.

Usage

xref live heap [OPTIONS] --pid <PID>

Arguments and options

Options

--pid <PID>
Target process ID.
--duration <DURATION>
How long to observe, e.g. 10m or 30s; also ends at process exit or Ctrl-C.
default 60s
--interval <INTERVAL>
Also write a snapshot every interval (e.g. 30s), to see which stacks grow.
--sample-bytes <SAMPLE_BYTES>
Keep one stack per this many mapped bytes (e.g. 4M); every mapping at least this large is kept exactly.
default 4M
--stack-bytes <STACK_BYTES>
User stack bytes copied with each memory syscall for DWARF unwinding.
default 8192
--out <OUT>
Directory (new) for the .xprof snapshots (heap-0001.xprof, ...); xref profile diff compares two.
--top <TOP>
Rows in the report.
default 30
--folded <FOLDED>
Also write folded stacks weighted by bytes (flame-graph input) to this new file.
--json
Print the capture statistics and the report as JSON.

Examples

Command
# Start the program, then attach at once: memory mapped before xref attaches is not attributed.
./server & sudo xref live heap --pid $! --duration 10m --out heap-run1
# Snapshots every 30 seconds show which stacks keep growing.
sudo xref live heap --pid 1234 --duration 30m --interval 30s --out heap-run2
# Compare two runs (before and after a change) stack by stack.
xref -b server profile diff heap-run1/heap-0001.xprof heap-run2/heap-0060.xprof

On a small C program that allocates 256 MiB in big() and 200,000 objects of 1000 bytes in small_many(), then frees a second 64 MiB block (library paths shortened):

live heap: 448.0 MiB mapped while observed (2953 memory syscalls, 38 lost, 1 threads, 4920 ms, stop process_exited)
stacks by live bytes (root -> leaf):
  256.0 MiB  57.14%  target:_start -> libc.so.6:fn_2a200 -> libc.so.6:fn_2a150 -> target:main -> target:phase -> target:big -> libc.so.6:fn_ad750 -> ...
  192.0 MiB  42.86%  target:_start -> libc.so.6:fn_2a200 -> libc.so.6:fn_2a150 -> target:main -> target:phase -> target:small_many -> libc.so.6:fn_ad750 -> ...

Reading the output

  • The first line is the bytes the reported stacks hold, the number of memory syscalls seen and lost, the threads followed and why the capture stopped.
  • stacks by live bytes lists whole call stacks, root first. The library frames below the program (the allocator: malloc and the syscall wrapper) are folded into one frame such as [libc.so.6], so the frame before it is the program's code that asked for the memory.
  • functions by live bytes adds up every stack a function of the program is on; library functions are left out, so the first rows are the program's.
  • With --interval, snapshots: shows the total at each snapshot. Each one is an .xprof recording in --out, whose sample weights are bytes, so profile diff compares two of them.
  • profile report on a snapshot ranks the same way, by bytes, with stacks and functions; --within FN lists the bytes under each direct callee of FN ((in FN) for what FN allocated itself), and --folded is weighted by bytes. Rust names are demangled, and functions can be named as reports print them:
Command
xref -b server profile report heap-run1/heap-0003.xprof --within "my_crate::state::State::load"

How bytes are attributed

  • An allocation at or above glibc's mmap threshold (128 KiB by default, raised up to 32 MiB after large frees) is its own mmap, so it is attributed exactly to the stack that allocated it, and its free (munmap) takes it back.
  • Smaller allocations reach the kernel only when an arena grows: brk for the main arena, mprotect inside the 64 MiB reservation of another arena. The malloc that crosses the boundary carries the stack, which samples small allocations by their bytes.
  • To keep long captures bounded, one stack is kept per --sample-bytes of mapped memory and stands for those bytes; every mapping at least that large is kept exactly.

Limits

  • Only memory mapped while xref observes is attributed. Attach when the process starts: a process at steady state makes no memory syscalls, and what it mapped earlier is not shown.
  • Freed small objects stay in their arena and are not returned to the kernel, so the small-allocation part is a high-water mark, not live objects. Arena memory a later malloc reuses is attributed to the stack that first grew it.
  • Needs root (or CAP_PERFMON with tracefs access) for the syscalls tracepoints. Function names need a symbol table; for a stripped Rust binary build with strip = false.
  • A burst of syscalls can overflow a ring: the first line counts lost events.
  • Allocators other than glibc (jemalloc, mimalloc) map memory in their own chunk sizes; the attribution still follows their syscalls.
